children: *Jungle Ventures Expects an IPO From Its Portfolio Every Six Months, Founding Partner Says
*Jungle Ventures Founder: 70% of India, Singapore Investments Are in AI, Advanced Manufacturing
*Jungle Ventures Aims to Set Up Office in Malaysia, Founding Partner Says
This Venture Capital Firm Wants a Listing Every Six Months — Interview
By Kimberley Kao

Getting the timing right for an initial public offering exit is a key concern for many venture-capital firms. Asia-focused Jungle Ventures has a more aggressive strategy, aiming for a listing every six months regardless of market conditions.

"A lot of people talk about how there's always been a window to go public. But I actually don't believe in it," said Amit Anand, founding partner of Singapore-based Jungle Ventures. "When you're solving robust problems and you build business profitability doing that, [it's] always a good time to go public."
Jungle Ventures manages a portfolio of roughly $1.5 billion in assets and invests in a range of startups across Asia.
It has maintained a loss ratio of less than 5% over the past 15 years, which Anand attributed to its focus on "margin before scale."

Jungle Ventures declined to give specific financial figures for individual portfolio companies, However, it said key investments in startups Moglix, Kredivo, Livspace and Sociolla have a combined revenue run-rate in a range of $1.7 billion to $2 billion.

Other companies it has backed include insurance-tech platform Turtlemint, which listed in India in June, and consumer-appliance maker Atomberg, which filed for an IPO last month. Jungle was also an early investor in fashion company Pomelo.
Jungle's largest pool of capital is in India, with a portfolio of businesses in Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam and Malaysia, where the firm hopes to set up an office, he said.

In the first half of the year, India had 12 IPO exits from private equity and venture capital investments totaling $801 million, marking a 47% decline compared with a year earlier, according to data from EY and the Indian Private Equity and Venture Capital Association. Despite near-term uncertainties, improving valuation levels and India's growth potential are expected to support an optimistic outlook for private equity and venture capital activity, EY said.
Nonetheless, Anand remains optimistic.
Returning investors re-committed 127% of their prior capital to the firm's latest fund, which underscores sustained appetite in India and Southeast Asia, Anand said.

Demand for assets in the region is further reflected in recent deal-making activity involving private equity giants like TPG and KKR, which see buying opportunities rather than a retreat from Asian investments, he said.
He identified advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence as particularly attractive sectors for VC in Asia, where 70% of Jungle's investments in India and Singapore are in.

Based on the opportunities that he sees in the market, Anand said there will be a wave of "completely homegrown" AI native services and semiconductor companies in Southeast Asia in the next four to five years.
When Jungle was founded more than two decades ago, most of the entrepreneurs it worked with in the region were inexperienced.

"Today, 70% are not first-time founders," Anand said. "You are no longer having to sit down and talk to entrepreneurs and help them appreciate the importance of prioritization of margin before scale or how to build a team that can build a regional company... they have an understanding of that."
That gives him more conviction about the success of Jungle's IPO exits.
"The measure of Jungle's success is going to be the hit rate in terms of the number of investments that have gone public from us," Anand said. "I'm hoping we will exceed the industry."
